In this context, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general framework encompassing a broad class of models. However, exploring the enormous space of possible SMEFT operators rapidly becomes a challenging combinatorial problem: many operators can contribute simultaneously to different observables, their effects are correlated, and distinct operator combinations can provide comparably good descriptions of the data. In this work, we formulate the exploration of the SMEFT operator space as a sequential decision-making problem using reinforcement learning (RL). Our RL agent employs a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters in total. Rather than searching for a single best-fit theory, our method is designed to discover a diverse set of high-quality theory hypotheses. We test the method in a complex phenomenological environment comprising 132 observables across several sectors of particle physics, including 24 measurements that deviate from their SM predictions by more than $1.5σ$. We show that the learned RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit. Comparisons with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches demonstrate the ability of the RL policy to navigate this large combinatorial space. Our results establish RL as a systematic framework for exploring diverse patterns of new physics (NP) interactions within SMEFT.

title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs
summary: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.

title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions
summary: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean framework that pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts, obtained through type class resolution when possible and otherwise defined separately with an equivalence proof. Test cases can then evaluate declarative specifications by execution, letting us use agreement as a reinforcement-learning reward. Using AuXSpec, we synthesize 3,037 LeetCode problems and expand training to 19.5K samples through expert iteration on Codeforces. Experiments show that training Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B with the execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test 0.7% $\to$ 82.7% and 14.3% $\to$ 84.3%, and the 27B model outperforms all frontier models. On the out-of-domain Verina benchmark with its original prompts, both models improve 7.0% $\to$ 90.5% and 21.9% $\to$ 90.5% and surpass VeriSpecGen-30B-A3B, the prior state of the art among open-source specification models, on pass@1 (theirs 47.6% vs. ours 73.7% and 84.5%) and pass@4 (theirs 63.9% at pass@10 vs. ours 90.5%). We release the weights of the trained 9B and 27B models and the 3,037 problems with test cases, including the 300-problem AuXSpec-Test benchmark with expert review and correctness proofs for future evaluation. Models and data: https://huggingface.co/collections/eth-algopt/auxspec. Website: https://auxspec.org

title: Reinforcement Learning designs Quantum Repeater Protocols on Networks beyond the Chain Scenario
summary: Small-scale quantum repeater protocols have been shown to distribute entanglement over existing telecommunication infrastructure by means of short range quantum communications and long range classical messages. For larger networks, there are a number of theoretical proposals about how to operate the network to achieve a good performance under varying metrics. Moreover, since the dimension of the space of possible protocols grows exponentially with network size, plenty of those proposals are based on heuristics that reduce the search space. One of these is entanglement routing, which simplifies the problem on non-linear networks by allocating a series of disjoint paths and running chain protocols simultaneously on them. However, in this work we claim routing leads to suboptimal protocols. In fact, inspired by works on linear chains, we apply reinforcement learning to non-linear networks and optimize over the larger non-routing protocol space. Then, we find protocols that outperform a routed extension of the swap-ASAP protocol, even in the parameter regimes where the latter is widely recognized as the state of the art. These results indicate that routing must be discarded in favor of non-routing methods, while they pave the way towards the design of a sensible Quantum Internet architecture.

title: Do Embedding-Map Distances Guide LLM Ideation? Four Tests Against What Came Next
summary: A popular ideation recipe treats an embedding map of existing work as a guide: pick points far from everything and decode them into ideas. I test four ways such distances could guide ideation against what appeared later. (1) Far random directions are not text: no later item reaches a raw cosine above about 0.10 with one (after centring or whitening, 22 of 24 cells stay out of reach), and an LLM decoder shown a target's neighbours, with score-only feedback, writes those neighbours in all six target sets. A neighbour-free search writes coherent text at median cosine 0.57 and 0.47 to interior gaps, beating the nearest existing item on 15 and 14 of 20, but only 0.07 and 0.06 to far points. (2) On k-means cells of a past-only map, the registered hole score mostly tracks cell size and position; three density-based gap scores forecast which cells grow fastest at or below chance (AUC 0.30 to 0.66) and add nothing to momentum in Steam and arXiv, with patents inconclusive; more isolated new Steam games are slightly better reviewed. (3) LLM continuations of arXiv papers stay closer to the source than papers that cite it, under three user prompts and against proposal rewrites (gpt-4o) and April-December 2023 papers (OLMo). Critique lengthens this step beyond content-free revision, replicated on 150 new papers. Revealing a real follow-up's title turns the ideas by 0.032 along a follow-up-specific direction beyond revision; reviewer, oracle and distance feedback add 0.13, 0.08 and 0.34 of that turn (upper bounds 0.46, 0.46, 0.70), and their turn is not separable from revision or their longer step. (4) For inspiration material graded by distance, no inverted U was detected, on an anticipation margin that tracks format more than content. Original tests were registered before running, follow-ups (thirteen requested in two AI-agent reviews) after the main results; all are dated only by local git commits.

title: Beyond Bilingual: Studying Quadrilingual Code-Switching with Conversational AI
summary: Multilingual speakers choose languages by topic and conversation partner. Large language models (LLMs) support these languages unequally. Research on code-switching with conversational AI has mostly examined bilingual pairs of well-resourced languages. In Curaçao and Aruba, many people use Dutch, English, Spanish, and the low-resource Creole Papiamentu/o. In a preregistered study, 42 university students held two five-minute chatbot conversations, one about university life and one about local food and culture. Surveys assessed language background, AI use, and switching comfort. 20 international students in Curaçao formed a comparison sample. Participants switched between turns and rarely mixed languages within a message. English dominated both conversations. Participants switched more often in the cultural conversation, where Papiamentu/o and Spanish rose from 15% to 24% of messages. Self-reports showed no lower comfort switching with the chatbot than with a person. Conversational agents must follow turn-by-turn language changes and handle local low-resource languages well.

title: Stability-Compensated Threshold Calibration for Selection-Conditioned Risk Control in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models often produce hallucinated answers, motivating selective prediction policies that abstain on uncertain queries. However, heuristic uncertainty thresholds alone do not provide statistical control of errors among accepted predictions. Linear Expectation Constraints (LEC) reduce selection-conditioned error rate (SCER) calibration to a nonpositive expected linear-loss constraint, but the associated loss is non-monotonic in the acceptance threshold. We construct an exact counterexample under i.i.d. sampling demonstrating that LEC's empirical threshold-selection rule can violate the population SCER target. To address this risk-transfer gap, we introduce Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control (SC-LEC), which uses the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference to compensate for threshold-selection instability. For local expansion beyond a safe anchor, we derive two finite-sample certificates: a stability-based certificate exploiting rank crossings and a direct certificate using the structure of threshold expansion to reduce conservatism. With a valid population anchor margin, our certificate conditions ensure finite-sample marginal SCER control, and independent margin certification further provides a $1-δ$ high-probability guarantee for this calibration-averaged control. Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show useful retention gains beyond the same certified anchor, while revealing conservative behavior in small-margin regimes.

title: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign
summary: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.

title: A Crowd-Audited Atlas of Implicit Bias in LLM-Powered Agents
summary: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) express implicit biases in high-publicity, one-off decision scenarios such as hiring and intelligence assessment. However, as people increasingly employ autonomous, LLM-powered AI agents that make decisions on their behalf in doing day-to-day tasks, it is of critical importance that we understand how implicit biases, based on sociodemographic assumptions, emerge across a broad milieu of workaday decision scenarios. We used the 17 domains of daily activity in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to generate an atlas of 506 decision scenarios in which LLMs --- endowed with personas representing different races, gender identities, and political ideologies --- expressed significant implicit bias. Next, in a crowdsourced audit, 500 participants made 8,010 binary choices about which implicitly biased decision scenarios most deserved further review. We found that participants prioritized decision scenarios that had broad relevance (e.g., about food choices), were high stakes (e.g., about health), and where all members of a simulated sociodemographic group made unanimous decisions (because it was a clear indication of stereotyping). They were less swayed by the magnitude of an observed disparity or the specific ATUS domain the decision scenario represented. When examining the rationale behind their prioritization choices, we found that participants often interpreted disparities as traits of demographic groups and judged whether those traits seemed plausible, often based on their own internalized stereotypes. We discuss implications for building personalized AI agents, digital twins, social simulations, and for using crowdsourced bias audits.

title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection
summary: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.

title: Federated TD Learning in Heterogeneous Environments with Average Rewards: A Two-timescale Approach with Polyak-Ruppert Averaging
summary: Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) provides a promising way to speedup training in reinforcement learning when one has access to multiple edge devices that can operate in parallel. Recently, it has been shown that even when these edge devices have access to different dynamic models---such as cars or robots with differing system configurations---an optimal convergence rate that has a linear speedup proportional to the number of devices is achievable. However, this result requires that the algorithm's stepsize be chosen in a manner that depends on the unknown model parameters. Also, it applies only to a discounted setting, which has been argued to fit episodic tasks better than continuing control tasks. In this paper, we obtain finite-time bounds for heterogeneous FRL with average rewards. We show that optimal convergence rate and linear speedup are achievable even with a universal stepsize choice, independent of the underlying dynamics. To achieve our result, we modify the existing one-timescale FRL method to a novel two-timescale variant that additionally incorporates iterate averaging. We remark that this idea also extends to other settings already studied in the literature, such as the homogeneous FRL or the heterogeneous case with a discounted cost function.

title: Premise Recovery in Software Design: What Does This Decision Rest On?
summary: Design decisions shape software architecture, and writing them down preserves the reasons behind it. Architecture decision records (ADRs) capture them, each with its context, choice, and consequences. A decision can depend on earlier ones: reversing one of them would force its review. We call these its premises. Yet ADRs do not always name their premises. When a decision is reversed, engineers supersede its ADR and search by hand for what it affects. That search can miss ADRs resting on an unnamed premise. We frame this as premise recovery: given an ADR with identifiers masked, find its premises among earlier records. We collect 1,060 ADRs from 36 repositories and label 1,529 candidate pairs for 60 target ADRs. Two LLM annotators agree at \k{appa} = 0.859. An independent human annotator, blind to their labels, agrees with the stated/implicit tag on 30 of 32 premises (\k{appa} = 0.875). We compare 7 open-weight models with 2 baselines that use no LLM. Qwen3.8-27B reaches F1 0.756, against 0.466 for word overlap; 2 models added post hoc score similarly. On the 11 premises whose titles barely overlap the target, it finds 0.758, while word overlap finds none. Reasoning raises its recall of implicit premises but not its F1. Word overlap with as many predictions gains 69% as much. We find only 2 to 3 stale dependents, though we searched for unlinked ones in only 30 of 66 supersessions. Open models could thus suggest unwritten premises when a decision is reversed, with precision between 0.68 and 0.78.

title: ALIVE: Making Streaming Video Models Interactive
summary: Streaming video LLMs can continuously observe the world, yet often handle user requests in isolation. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model supporting proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning teaches when and how to respond, while reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses, and silence across multi-turn interactions. We also introduce FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback seeking and subsequent task completion. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.

title: Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion for Decomposable Generative Models
summary: Generative model pre-training typically optimizes a model as a whole without explicitly organizing its parameters for selective reuse. Decomposable pre-training instead learns reusable components for downstream adaptation while retaining strong generative performance. However, existing knowledge diversion methods incur substantial parameter overhead through weight factorization and rely on fixed component assignments to induce specialization, potentially compromising in-distribution generation quality. We therefore propose Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion (SGKDiv), which learns how generative knowledge is shared and specialized for effective generation and selective downstream reuse. SGKDiv constructs Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels, preserving native computational structure without SVD-based reparameterization. Calibrated condition-wise routing combines a shared usage prior with conditional adjustments, while complementary regularization shapes their allocation, diversity, and magnitude. Together, these designs replace predefined component assignments with adaptively learned and explicitly regulated knowledge specialization. Experiments across diverse model and training settings demonstrate better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines, alongside stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.

title: Representational Change Under Self-Consuming Training: A Sparse Autoencoder Analysis
summary: Large language models are increasingly exposed to model-generated text, raising the possibility that future models will be trained recursively on the outputs of their predecessors. Prior work on such self-consuming training loops has largely focused on output quality and downstream performance, leaving their effects on internal representations poorly understood. We study how representations evolve across five generations of self-consumption and whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) remain reliable under this shift. At each generation, we compare a lineage trained on synthetic data with a matched control trained on real data under the same training settings. We evaluate how well SAEs trained before self-consumption transfer to later generations, measuring reconstruction and sparsity across SAE widths, architectures, and model layers. We then fine-tune the original SAE on each generation and use sparse probing to test whether task-relevant information remains concentrated in a small number of latents or becomes more distributed across the representation. We find that zero-shot SAE performance degrades progressively under self-consumption, with growing reconstruction and sparsity gaps that vary substantially across layers. Fine-tuning largely restores reconstruction, but not feature-level usefulness: task-relevant information remains accessible in the full latent space while becoming less concentrated in individual features. These results show that self-consumption induces representational drift and that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient to establish that an adapted SAE remains equally useful for interpretation.

title: Generating a simple silicon detector simulation with an open-weight large language model
summary: Recent LLM developments have seen AI-generated code become commonplace in the software development industry. Without tool access, LLMs cannot execute simulations, and their knowledge of toolkits such as Geant4 is limited. We demonstrate here, a detector simulation workflow with a Qwen3.6-27B model with Q4_K_M GGUF quantisation together with custom resources and tools served via MCP servers to generate a particle detector simulation. In 50 independent runs, 42(29--56)% at 95% CI produced energy-deposit distributions statistically consistent with a reference simulation, measured against a reference simulation. These results provide a proof of concept that MC simulations can be generated using text-based prompts with an LLM, given the necessary resources and tools. More extensive resources, such as example code and additional documentation, are likely to be required for more complex simulation tasks.

title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models
summary: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.

title: Can AI Mature a Model's Geometry? Training-Free Weight Baking in LLMs
summary: Can an AI make a trained language model more mature, in the sense of a better organized latent space, by looking only at the geometry of that space? An analyst model reads a fixed-size digest of topological descriptors of the layers of a frozen target and proposes a transformation, which closed-form ridge regression writes into the feed-forward weights without gradient training. Using lightweight models, 126 runs show that category purity rose on unseen words and sentences, benchmark accuracy stayed within sampling error, and the analyst matched a category-aware heuristic with gentler edits. In a five-model round robin approach, 16 pairs raised purity and four left the target unchanged. The results provide a baseline for future work on LLM-guided, training-free model editing without using raw weights.

title: LATTE-WordSeg-Lite: Multi-Granularity Thai Word Segmentation on a CPU, with a Reproducible Benchmark
summary: Large language models read Thai through subword tokens, without a word segmenter. Yet Thai treebanks, speech metrics and morphological resources are built on words, often at several granularities, and word boundaries resolve ambiguities that subword tokens leave open. LATTE (Lattice ATTentive Encoding) reads a text at several granularities at once, through a lattice of dictionary words, but it is a large GPU model. We distil it into LATTE-WordSeg-Lite, a CPU segmenter of 1.17M parameters that keeps the lattice as features. It outputs compounds, words and morphemes in one pass, and learns only from annotated data and text whose licences allow commercial use. To compare it with other tools, published Thai scores do not suffice, as they come from different files, splits and scorers. We therefore rebuild seven test sets from pinned sources and score twelve systems under one protocol. With the unit that fits each test set, LATTE-WordSeg-Lite scores above DeepCut on five sets, four of them from corpora that its teachers learnt from. Called line by line on one CPU thread, it runs 23 times as fast as DeepCut. We release the model, the benchmark scripts and all predictions.

title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.

title: Agent-Native by Design: A Programming Language for Agentic Applications
summary: Building agentic applications requires combining large language model (LLM) operations, workflow structure and application state, and model-guided routing. With SDKs and agent frameworks, developers connect these components through supporting code that prepares model inputs, propagates state, and dispatches model-selected steps. Workflow changes can require coordinated updates to this code, increasing development and testing effort. Splitting execution logic between application code and framework internals also limits compiler visibility into control flow and state dependencies, hindering automatic optimization. We introduce Agent-Native Programming, which unifies these three components with shared execution semantics. We realize this approach in Jac, a Python-superset language, through "by llm()" for typed model operations and tool use, Object-Spatial Programming for workflow structure and state, and "visit ... by llm()" for model-guided routing. The routing construct derives the model's choices from executable workflow steps and schedules the selected steps. This explicit connection between model decisions and program execution gives the compiler and runtime a common basis for dependency analysis and automatic optimization. Across five benchmarks and five baselines, Jac achieves a 1.8-8.7x reduction in AI-integration code relative to the OpenAI SDK, with competitive observed task quality and lower coding-agent development effort. Two case studies demonstrate speculative execution and service partitioning through configuration alone, using program analysis and runtime checks to preserve workflow behavior under stated conditions.

title: Deep Learning for Physicists: From Linear Regression to Reasoning Models
summary:
These lecture notes are based on an introductory course on neural networks and deep learning that the author taught in the School of Mathematical Sciences at Queen Mary University of London in 2023/24 and 2024/25. The author, however, is a physicist, and it shows: wherever possible, ideas are explained with physical intuition rather than heavy formalism. Readers with a background in physics or mathematics who want a self-contained, introductory route into modern machine learning may therefore find these notes particularly friendly.
  The notes start from maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression and (stochastic) gradient descent. They then cover neural networks, backpropagation, the vanishing gradient problem, batch and layer normalization, overfitting and regularization, adversarial examples, and the kernel method. The second half turns to natural language processing: word embeddings, recurrent networks and LSTMs, the attention mechanism and Transformers, and large language models, including scaling laws, the history of GPT, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning and test-time scaling. The emphasis on large language models reflects requests from the students.
  The notes are aimed at third- and fourth-year students in the UK system. Because the course was also taken by students from other departments, very little is assumed: even basic material such as matrix multiplication is explained from scratch, so readers familiar with it can safely skip such parts. No originality is claimed; the aim is a coherent, intuitive path through the material. Developments after spring 2025 are not covered, but the basic ideas emphasized here are unlikely to go out of date soon.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation
summary: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at dhaibench.silent3.ff.cuni.cz.

title: FM-Recon: Exploring Foundation Model Features for Accelerated Cardiac Cine MRI Reconstruction
summary: Foundation models have demonstrated strong feature extraction capabilities across various medical imaging tasks, yet their potential for MRI reconstruction remains largely unexplored, particularly within unrolled reconstruction networks and under artifact-corrupted inputs. In this work, we explore whether and how features from pretrained foundation models can benefit accelerated cardiac cine MRI reconstruction. To this end, we propose FM-Recon, a framework that refines and integrates extracted features from frozen image encoder of foundation models into an unrolled reconstruction network. Through extensive experiments on the CMRxRecon2023 dataset, we systematically evaluate foundation model features across different reconstruction settings. Our results show that foundation models can extract informative representations from artifact-corrupted inputs and improve reconstruction performance, particularly at moderate acceleration factors. These findings demonstrate the potential of foundation model features for accelerated MRI reconstruction and provide insights into their effective integration into unrolled reconstruction networks.

title: SURMA: Efficient Fine-Grained Communication Offload for SuperPOD
summary: GPU SuperPODs underpin large language model (LLM) serving, but growing bandwidth and round-trip times make inter-GPU communication consume increasing compute resources. SM-driven remote memory access occupies shared memory or registers for in-flight data and competes for SM-to-NoC bandwidth. Dedicated engines can free these resources, but must handle fine-grained transfers, down to a 576\,B KV-cache entry. NVIDIA's CopyEngine uses less than 1\% of NVLink bandwidth at 7\,KB granularity. We present SURMA, an on-die Scale-Up Remote Memory Access engine. Adapting RDMA requires overcoming slow doorbell submission, excessive per-application connection state, head-of-line blocking of completion notifications on shared connections, and costly ordering for multipath transfers. SURMA uses a credit-based shared send queue to reduce submission latency from 1.2\,$μ$s to 400\,ns; fused write-with-atomic semantics to share connections while independently notifying each transaction; and Network Per Path Ordering to ensure data arrives before the completion flag without Sender or Receiver Ordering. We implement SURMA in RTL on a two-FPGA prototype and evaluate it with two 8-GPU NVLink servers. At 512\,B granularity, SURMA saturates attainable bandwidth with a single SM, whereas NVLink needs over 14\% of the SMs. SURMA occupies under 0.5\% of GPU area and accelerates inference on four models by 1.05--1.26$\times$ over NVLink.

title: Certified Nash Equilibrium Learning for Nonzero-Sum Jump-Diffusion Games: Policy Iteration and Off-Policy Q-Learning
summary: This paper establishes two model-free reinforcement learning methods for infinite-horizon N-player linear-quadratic nonzero-sum stochastic differential games whose drift, Brownian diffusion, and Poisson jump amplitudes depend on all players' controls. Control dependence in the diffusion and jump terms couples the players' simultaneous feedback updates. A verifiable certificate ensures that the partially model-free policy iteration map is contractive on an invariant closed ball centered at an admissible initial feedback profile. All feedback iterates are mean-square stabilizing, and the algorithm achieves local geometric convergence of feedback gains and value matrices to those associated with a closed-loop Nash equilibrium. The term certified refers to a verifiable convergence certificate that guarantees mean-square stability of all policy iterates and local geometric convergence to a closed-loop Nash equilibrium. To implement the policy updates from data, the off-policy Q-learning algorithm reuses the same behavior-policy data across iterations without requiring the system coefficients or jump intensity. Under quantitative persistence of excitation and a common initialization, exact population regression reproduces the policy-iteration sequence. The same local convergence guarantee therefore applies to off-policy Q-learning at the population level. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the two proposed algorithms.

title: In-Context Estimation and Prediction for Parametric ODEs
summary: Transformers have demonstrated the ability to perform in-context learning, that is, to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without updating their parameters. Existing theory has largely focused on emulating gradient-based algorithms for convex statistical problems or establishing general function approximation guarantees without exploiting the underlying statistical structure. We study in-context parameter estimation and trajectory prediction for parametric ordinary differential equations (ODEs), where estimation is generally nonconvex. Under suitable identifiability and regularity conditions, we construct a transformer that estimates unknown system parameters from noisy trajectory observations through a two-stage approximate maximum likelihood procedure: a coarse search provides an initialization within a locally strongly convex region, followed by gradient descent with local linear contraction. For prediction, we compose this estimator with a neural approximation of the ODE solution map. We further show that, through parameter sharing, a single transformer can perform both parameter estimation and trajectory prediction simultaneously. For these constructions, we establish nonasymptotic guarantees and finite-pretraining oracle inequalities that separate errors due to finite pretraining data, finite context length, and finite-sized transformer approximation. Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear ODEs further show that pretrained transformers can benefit from longer inference contexts without updating their weights.

title: Variance-adaptive confidence regions for fixed-benchmark binomial mixtures, with application to LLM evaluation
summary: We construct confidence intervals for linear functionals $θ(F_m)=\int h\,dF_m$ of the empirical law $F_m$ of success probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_m$, from independent counts $c_i\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p_i)$, as for a language model run $n$ times per problem. Coverage is at least $1-α$ for every $n$, $m$ and fixed $(p_i)$, simultaneously for all bounded $h$. The variance-adaptive (VA) region tests each candidate mixing law with the conditional variance of the tail counts it implies. This variance is linear in the law, so the region is a linear program, and cell envelopes keep it valid off-grid. Regions calibrated for iid sampling target a super-population law and are conservative for $θ(F_m)$. With all $n$ tail counts, fixed $n$, continuous $h$ and a grid refined as $m\to\infty$, the identification part of VA's width is first-order worst-case optimal, as for any localization with the same index set. Under a rule fixed before the main comparator runs, VA was narrower than a two-stage plug-in band at every $n$ (median width ratio 0.60 at $n=128$), but not than the asymptotic, pointwise AMARI interval at $n=128$; on real rollout pools it was wider than both pointwise and Bonferroni-adjusted AMARI at $n\le128$. For $P(p>0)$ and pass@$k$ with $k\gg n$ the data support only lower bounds.

title: Evaluating Authorization and Trust Boundaries in Agentic Orchestration Frameworks
summary: Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, and multi-agent collaboration, introducing security risks at orchestration boundaries. These risks depend on how identities are represented, operations are authorized, and instructions or information propagate between components. We evaluate LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, and OpenClaw through twelve experiments mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications using a common LLM (gpt-4o-mini). The experiments cover prompt injection, unauthorized resource access and command execution, memory poisoning, and inter-agent trust and identity attacks. Adversarial inputs induced unauthorized tool invocation, while tool chaining, stale filesystem validation, encoded instructions, and inter-agent delegation exposed weaknesses in authorization across component boundaries. Memory poisoning showed that untrusted state can influence responses, a risk distinct from conventional access-control violations. In the evaluated protected configurations, explicit authorization, controlled capability assignment, filesystem containment, and execution safeguards prevented specific unauthorized operations. The findings emphasize preserving authorization and information-trust boundaries throughout agentic workflows rather than treating framework capabilities or model-level instructions as sufficient security guarantees.

title: Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning for Sample Efficient Experimentation
summary: Self-driving laboratories must learn to control a process from tens to hundreds of expensive experiments, too few for deep reinforcement learning (RL). We learn the Q-function directly with a Gaussian process (GP), which avoids learning the dynamics, and show that the GP posterior supplies the learning rate of Q-learning. If each Bellman target is treated as a noisy measurement of the Q-function, the learning rate that minimises the mean squared error is the Kalman gain, and applying it to every observed transition is equivalent to GP regression. Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning (HGPQ) sets the noise variance of each target with a heteroscedastic GP, which learns how unreliable the targets are across the states and inputs. Targets from noisy operating conditions, or from regions where the value function has large gradients, then move the estimate less than targets from low-noise regions, so HGPQ learns quickly where the data are reliable without being misled where they are not. For kernel value iteration with per-target variances that are assigned when a target is collected, we prove a high-probability bound on the error of the value estimate, uniform over the explored region. Pooled over five simulated benchmarks, which include a chemical reactor and a bioprocess, HGPQ approaches the best return found by any method in fewer episodes than GP, kernel and deep RL baselines.

title: How Developer Personality Shapes the Use of AI Coding Assistants
summary:
Developers differ in personality traits that shape how they approach software development tasks, yet AI coding assistants either behave uniformly or offer personalization features whose fit with individual developers must be found through trial and error. This is because it remains unclear how personality shapes developers' experiences with AI assistants, and thus which traits personalization should account for. In other words, we provide tools with no underlying theory on what works when and why. We take a first step towards such a theory with a systematic scoping review on how users' personality relates to their perception of LLM-based tools. We identified twelve studies through general search engines, major Software Engineering (SE) venues, AI tooling, and snowballing. They all reported associations between personality and perceptions, particularly perceived usefulness, yet none addressed this in a SE context.
  Building on these findings, we conducted an exploratory two-wave survey with 29 and 11 developers, collecting first empirical evidence of how developers' personality (measured using the Big Five Model) relates to the perception of AI coding assistants. Higher Extraversion was associated with more positive private-use experiences in both waves, while Agreeableness was associated with negative professional experiences in the first wave and positive ones in the second. These results provide first indications that the personality effects found in the literature extend to developers. Although further studies with bigger samples are needed to build a theory, our work takes the first step towards an empirical grounded theory of developer personality and AI personalization traits.

title: A Generative AI-Driven Architecture for Whole-Home Intelligent Services: Edge Models, Memory Management, and Household Applications
summary: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.

title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
summary: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

title: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression
summary: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.

title: Open-fMIND: A Large-Scale Open-Access fMRI Corpus for Pretraining Brain Foundation Models
summary: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its application to functional MRI (fMRI) is constrained by data access. The largest standardized fMRI resources are governed by data use agreements and dominated by a small number of acquisition protocols, while the thousands of openly licensed datasets on OpenNeuro are individually small, heterogeneously organized, and unprocessed. We present the first release of Open-fMIND, a uniformly preprocessed, openly accessible corpus of parcellated fMRI timeseries from 322 OpenNeuro studies, comprising 11,379 subjects and 45,731 functional runs. Each run is preprocessed with fMRIPrep and parcellated under 52 atlases spanning 14 families, yielding a massive 2.4 million timeseries. Timeseries are released either denoised with our default pipeline (preproc) or as the fMRIPrep output with its confound files (quasiraw), with functional connectivity matrices, per-run provenance and motion metadata. Open-fMIND is intended as a pretraining resource for self-supervised brain representation learning. Pretraining on it yields downstream performance comparable to that obtained with UK Biobank.

title: Validating LLM-Based Essay Scorers: A Comparative Analysis in Critical Online Reasoning in Medical Education
summary: Automated essay scorers (AES) based on large language models (LLMs) promise human-level accuracy. However, training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs for specific assessment tasks is costly. In particular, the question arises whether these AES should be trained for specific domains or whether models based on generic LLMs might be sufficient. Human annotations, by contrast, are often more valid but far more expensive. This study evaluates whether ensembles of AES systems based on general-purpose LLMs can approximate human ratings of medical-education writing tasks by leveraging encoded linguistic and conceptual knowledge. The goal is to assess whether general-purpose models are applicable for assisting or potentially replacing human annotation in this domain. We experiment with 11 AES systems and 8 different LLMs and evaluate 668 student responses to 12 tasks, using \numprint{2076} evaluations by 7 human annotators. These ratings are aggregated to create consistent performance levels that can be used as target classes for classifiers trained on AES outputs. Our results show that learner classes based on human ratings can be accurately reconstructed using a linear SVM trained on a small set of AES features. A single classifier generalized well across tasks and domains, with reasoning and content features being most predictive. This suggests that out-of-the-box LLMs, even without domain-specific fine-tuning, can support automatic essay grading in medical education. While individual AES systems are insufficient alone, their combination approximates human evaluators, pointing to a reduced need for manual scoring or its supplementation with automated methods.

title: Who Is the Regression About? Auditing AI-Labeled Treatments When Effects Differ
summary: Researchers increasingly regress outcomes on treatments labeled by large language models. When effects differ, OLS averages the effect on the treated (ATT) and on the untreated (ATU), weighting the smaller group more. A label's bias then has two parts: classical attenuation from misclassification, and a selective term when its errors are correlated with the outcome. In LinkedIn postings, the model misses better-paid remote jobs: a precision check passes, yet the remote pay gap is understated by nearly 40 percent, a bias that more data cannot remove. A stratified, blind audit of both labeled groups corrects it and recovers both effects.

title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis
summary: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential route to automating scientific programming, but their usefulness depends on consistently producing numerically correct code. We extend FEM-Bench to 17 finite element tasks involving nonlinear and history-dependent mechanics and structural dynamics, and evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation without execution feedback. The best model succeeds in 87.1% of single-pass implementation trials, but rankings differ between tracks. The leading implementer achieves 49.9% joint test success, while the leading tester reaches 82.6%. For six models, we compare single-pass generation with two agentic harnesses that allow code execution and revision. Agentic execution solves some tasks that never succeeded in single-pass trials and improves consistency on others, but gains vary across models and harnesses, and regressions also occur. Claude Opus 5 with SimpleAgent reaches 96.5% Pass@3, the probability of at least one success in three attempts, but 77.1% Pass$^3$, the probability that all three succeed. No model-harness combination exceeds 78.8% Pass$^3$. To understand why agents submit incorrect code after passing their own checks, we analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and identify six categories of self-verification failure. The most common are inadequate test coverage (73.1%) and reliance on generic consistency checks (70.3%), and in 28.5% of cases the tests share an error with the implementation. Motivated by these findings, an exploratory configuration with separate coder and tester agents achieves the highest observed scores, with 97.6% Pass@3 and 88.8% Pass$^3$. These results identify consistency across attempts and independent verification as the main obstacles to trusting LLM-generated scientific code.

title: Beyond Token Stacking: Multi-scale Visual Modulation and Adaptive Fused-feature Calibration for MLLMs
summary: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced rapidly and follow two main paradigms: one involves concatenating visual and textual tokens for input into Large Language Model (LLM), while the other injects visual knowledge into Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) of the LLM. However, the former introduces a large number of redundant visual tokens, substantially increasing computational overhead. The latter reduces sequence length but removes images from the input stage entirely, which may hinder the activation of image-related knowledge. Moreover, naively injecting visual knowledge into the FFNs could induce activation distribution shifts due to cross-modal semantic discrepancies. To address these challenges, we develop Beyond Token Stacking (BTS), a novel visual enhancement framework for MLLMs. Specifically, we propose a Multi-scale Visual Modulation (MVM) mechanism that injects multi-scale visual information at the input stage via modulation without increasing the token sequence length. Furthermore, we develop an Adaptive Fused-feature Calibration (AFC) module that performs per-channel affine calibration to decouple visual injection from distribution alignment in the FFN layers, improving multimodal fusion stability while preserving language priors. Experiments show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: A Matter of Stages: Energy-Latency Trade-offs in Multimodal LLM Serving
summary: Online serving of multimodal large language models requires deciding whether to separate visual encoding (E), prefill (P), and decode (D) across GPUs and how to configure their frequencies. EPD disaggregation enables independent stage control, but it also changes communication and queueing behavior. Lowering one stage's frequency can increase queueing and prolong execution across the EPD pipeline. Consequently, reducing power at one stage does not necessarily reduce total GPU energy per request. In this paper, we systematically characterize fused and EPD-disaggregated serving across four multimodal models under a fixed three-GPU budget, followed by single-stage and uniform downclocking experiments across 18 workload combinations. We find that disaggregation reduces GPU energy per successful request by 13.3-37.0% at nearly identical output-token throughput, but increases mean TTFT. Downclocking exhibits distinct stage sensitivities, and aggressive frequency reductions can offset power savings through queueing and longer execution. Across the evaluated workloads, uniform downclocking to 80% reduces GPU energy by 11.7-18.6% with modest mean-latency changes. Guided by these findings, we develop a budgeted frequency exploration strategy to select energy-efficient configurations under latency constraints. Evaluation shows that four probes can identify the lowest-energy feasible configuration among 25 measured candidates across all 288 evaluated positive-margin SLO scenarios. These results provide practical guidance for energy-efficient multimodal serving.

title: DRaGAN: Dynamic Graph Attention Network for Multi-Radar Point Cloud Encoding in Automotive Radar Perception
summary: Radar represents a key modality for weather-robust perception. Unlike optical sensors such as camera and LiDAR, radar can penetrate fog, rain and snow due to its longer wavelength, and recent hardware advances have steadily improved its spatial resolution, thus making it increasingly relevant for autonomous systems. While processing raw radar data requires substantial memory computation, most existing work has focused on preprocessed point-cloud data similar to LiDAR. However, the sparse radar points and sensor-relative anisotropy make LiDAR-oriented encoders suboptimal. To address this problem, we present DRaGAN, a dynamic graph attention network for multi-radar point clouds. DRaGAN introduces a sensor-relative Fourier encoding of angle and range to capture fixed-aperture radar characteristics, gated short- and long-range hub nodes along each sensor's line of sight for efficient local-global message passing, and attention-guided dynamic rewiring that prunes weak edges and adds a bounded number of latent connections restricted to two-hop neighborhoods. This reduces the number of processed edges in deeper layers while preserving representation quality. On TruckScenes, DRaGAN improves test NDS by 10.10 points over the evaluated RadarGNN baseline and reduces the reported model FLOP count by 63.7%. This trade-off includes an increase in model latency from 40 to 53.16 ms and in trainable parameters from 1.2M to 1.7M on the evaluated implementations. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/chr-is-tof/DRaGAN.

title: Edit Recommendation: Can LLMs Anticipate Edit Requests from Users, and When?
summary: After a large language model (LLM) agent generates an artifact, users often send edit requests for it. This paper studies whether an LLM can anticipate these requests before they are sent. Such anticipation is useful in practice because it reduces the effort of user review and feedback. We formalize this task as edit recommendation and build EditRecBench, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs on this task, from real-world conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M. Through benchmarking and failure analysis, we identify a practical challenge that some cases are inherently difficult to predict in real-world settings. To address this, we introduce decision model-based gating to filter out cases where predictions are unlikely to be correct before they are presented to the user. Our trained model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown suggestions by 12--25 points at a gating threshold. Our code is available at https://github.com/ntt-dkiku/llm-edit-recommendation.

title: WinDEX: Metric 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild for Dexterous Teleoperation and Policy Learning
summary: Human manipulation data are widely used to train robots for human-like dexterity. However, low-cost, large-scale collection in the wild remains challenging. Existing methods remain limited in geometrically grounded metric-scale reconstruction, real-world generalization and inference speed. We present WinDEX, integrating (1) geometric-temporal optimization for metric 3D hand annotation from in-the-wild egocentric stereo videos, combined with visual-inertial SLAM for world-frame reconstruction; (2) WinDEX-Net, an end-to-end, fisheye-native network combining calibrated stereo, local detail and temporal context, with a data-model flywheel of model-assisted annotation and retraining; (3) distilled models for offline reconstruction and causal streaming, supporting reinforcement learning and teleoperation; and (4) low-cost CyberCap stereo-inertial capture, forming the WinDEX-Hand dataset with 1,000 hours of training annotations and held-out human-annotated in-the-wild 2D and independent optical motion-capture evaluation sets. Offline reconstruction runs at 43.61 FPS and causal streaming at 171 FPS. On held-out data, offline reconstruction achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: 14.5 pixels in-the-wild reprojection error and, with visual-inertial odometry, 37.29 mm world-frame joint error. We achieve 7.6 and 3.6 times the task success rates of reinforcement learning policies trained with WiLoR and HaWoR motion references, respectively, and demonstrate real-time arm-hand teleoperation. Project website: https://fruitrabbit.github.io/WinDEX/.

title: Scribble Once, Segment the Sequence: Bidirectional Temporal Consistency for Weakly Supervised Segmentation in Echocardiography Sequences
summary: Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations. Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this by offering transferable spatial representations with low trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this, we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders present in the mean-teacher architecture. Furthermore, a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder. Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework for scalable clinical deployment.

title: Linglong Agent Service: A Runtime for Centralized Agent Reasoning and Distributed Execution
summary: LLM agents can use remote tools and cloud sandboxes, but integrating reasoning, session state, and heterogeneous execution sites remains a runtime design problem. We present Linglong Agent Service (agentsvc), a self-hosted HTTP service and embeddable Python runtime that treats execution site as a configurable dimension alongside model, tools, and context. A parent service retains inference orchestration, tool descriptions, and conversation history; each inference request selects one child environment for file, shell, terminal, and MCP operations. Direct HTTP and child-initiated WebSocket tunnels carry the same application interfaces, including portable request context and centrally managed updates. The normal core path requires no third-party Python packages, with an optional Windows pseudo-terminal dependency. We further present online_debugger as the process-scale special case of execution-site separation: an instrumented program submits exception evidence, executes session-scoped inspection tools inside the incident process, and resumes the same diagnostic session. Its default prompt requires failing-then-passing reproduction evidence for source changes, while runtime patch activation and failed-call recovery remain unimplemented. We explain the design through constrained expected-utility reasoning, compare concrete mechanisms with Hermes Agent, Pi, Codex, and Claude Code, and report implementation and regression-test evidence. The current evidence establishes executable contracts, not performance advantages, repair accuracy, or production recovery. The source code is open source under the MIT license at https://github.com/mz24cn/agents.

title: The Limits of Closed-Form Couplings for Few-Step Generation
summary: Few-step generators via flow models require complicated technical solutions such as a pretrained flow model or a consistency loss. While rectified flows have gained popularity for their success in few-step sampling, they pay a cost of needing a pre-trained model and sampling a large number of couplings per dataset. Yet for a finite dataset and a Gaussian probability path, the probability-flow vector field of the empirical distribution is available in closed form, so one could use this field as the teacher and skip pretraining altogether. We demonstrate that, surprisingly, this approach is impossible for problems of practical relevance. In particular, the analytic solution of the diffusion process in high dimensions becomes almost a linear transformation. The integration returns the noise vector drawn at initialisation, plus a drift that is empirically a faint copy of the data point, almost independent of the noise. The coupling therefore differs from an independent pairing only through this drift. As a result, training a model on these couplings is almost equivalent to training the model on the independent draws of the noise and the data, which does not provide a useful teacher. We highlight that this is the direct consequence of the high-dimensionality of the data, and that for low enough dimensions or large enough datasets, analytic couplings become more efficient teachers. We quantify this effect by the fraction of endpoint energy carried by the drift, which scales as $\frac{\log N}{d}$ for a dataset of size $N$ in a $d$-dimensional space. Finally, we provide an empirical study confirming all the theoretical results presented in the paper.

title: Out-of-training properties in frozen interatomic potential embeddings are decodable and ordered by physical scale
summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are trained on energies, forces and stresses, yet their frozen representations can predict other materials properties. We probe ORB-v3 and UMA-S across layers, read-outs and equivariant channels for nine properties of 154,875 Materials Project crystals. Both models outperform composition-only descriptors on all targets, including five outside their training objectives; errors in physical units help assess potential screening applications. Optimal depth varies by property, consistent with a physical-scale ordering. Random-weight controls reveal strongly property-dependent benefits of pretraining. UMA-S's rotation-invariant angular channels improve crystal-system classification, while higher scores from its full tensor disappear under rotation; matched-model controls do not isolate equivariance as the explanation. Accuracy varies across different probes, but nearest-neighbour prediction often approaches XGBoost performance, even though materials do not form distinct clusters according to their properties. We also test whether a linear predictor trained on one model's embeddings can predict properties using the other model's embeddings after a learned linear transformation. Predictive accuracy is largely preserved, despite differences in which atoms the two models place close together. These results guide the reuse of frozen MLIP representations for materials prediction.

title: CivilBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Information Integration in Civil Engineering
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), is increasingly applied in civil and structural engineering for disaster assessment, structural analysis, and engineering decision support. However, the extent to which current VLMs possess the reasoning capabilities required for reliable engineering judgments remains unclear. In this work, we introduce CivilBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs in civil engineering and disaster-related scenarios. CivilBench covers three major task families: Sequential Reasoning, Image-based Structural Understanding, and Open-world Understanding, encompassing numerical reasoning, structural damage assessment, risk inference, causal analysis, and repair planning. The benchmark is constructed through a systematic pipeline of domain-specific data collection, engineering-oriented captioning, expert annotation, question design, and quality verification. Evaluation of representative state-of-the-art VLMs reveals substantial limitations in domain-specific reasoning, with Sequential Reasoning emerging as a major bottleneck, particularly when models must infer numerical relationships from sparse structured observations. Further experiments show that numerical priors and external knowledge can alleviate these limitations, although their effectiveness depends on the model's ability to reliably interpret and use the available evidence. CivilBench provides a capability-oriented testbed for identifying reasoning limitations and evaluating progress toward reliable AI-assisted engineering decision-making. The benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/traceuryuan/CivilBench.

title: MedicalDPO: Multi-Objective Direct Preference Optimization for CT to PET Translation
summary: CT-to-PET synthesis estimates functional PET images from anatomical CT scans for auxiliary analysis, representation pretraining, and missing-modality completion. Brownian Bridge diffusion models can produce multiple PET candidates of different quality under the same CT condition, exposing an intra-condition quality hierarchy. Candidate quality spans complementary spatial, structural, and intensity dimensions, while DPO-only fine-tuning may compromise absolute synthesis fidelity. We propose MedicalDPO which converts this hierarchy into preference supervision automatically constructed from paired CT-PET training data. Multiple candidates are ranked across the three fidelity dimensions, and strict cross-metric verification retains preferred-rejected pairs with consistent quality separation. Relative denoising-error preference optimization is jointly trained with the original Brownian Bridge objective to anchor the pretrained CT-to-PET mapping, while condition-balanced multi-pair rotation distributes preference supervision across CT conditions. Experiments on BBDM and CPDM show improvements across LPIPS, MAE, SSIM, and PSNR. Further analyses demonstrate metric complementarity and clear pair separation, while ablations show that the original training objective prevents the substantial degradation caused by DPO-only fine-tuning.

title: SWE-WhatIf: Simulating Real Users of Coding Agents from Recorded Session
summary: Recorded sessions between users and coding agents offer a way to evaluate how agents complete real-world tasks and interact with users. However, these sessions cannot simply be replayed with new agents, because recorded user replies may no longer apply when an agent takes a different trajectory. We introduce SWE-WhatIf, which replays recorded sessions with new agents by modeling the user's intents, the criteria for satisfying them, and the conditions under which they arise. Using this model, a user simulator generates replies that adapt to unseen agent turns while remaining grounded in the recording. Across 89 real-world sessions, SWE-WhatIf generated the replies most similar to those of real users and matched the strongest baseline when sessions were rewritten. To test adaptation, we replay sessions with agents instructed to avoid or repeat actions that the recorded user pushed back on. SWE-WhatIf produced the highest win rate for avoiding these actions (66.3%), significantly above chance. We further demonstrate its utility by ranking five LLMs as coding agents, where the highest-ranked model depended on how users specified and developed their intents, and a study with 16 users, where replaying their own sessions changed 14 participants' rankings and informed their future agent use.

title: Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Aligned Action Spaces for Cross-Game Generalization
summary: Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates. While multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) mitigates offline exposure bias and single-game reinforcement learning (RL) overfitting, scaling it to autoregressive VLMs faces two bottlenecks. First, token-to-action misalignment from subword length bias distorts discrete action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Second, multi-teacher policy conflict arises as source teachers under incompatible dynamics issue contradictory closed-loop corrections, causing negative transfer. We propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), a post-training framework that resolves multi-teacher policy conflict within an aligned semantic action space. CAMOPD first uses complete-action alignment to normalize command completion likelihoods over each game's legal action set, forming a calibrated categorical policy that provides reliable uncertainty margins for selective on-policy retention and visual specialist probes that can be evaluated across source games. To resolve policy conflict without target-game data, conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates these specialists across source games to capture both visual identifiability and inter-teacher compatibility, upweighting compatible teachers while suppressing conflicting corrections. On GameWorld's temporal and directional transfer suites with Qwen3.5-4B, CAMOPD achieves 26/30 (86.7%) and 24/30 (80.0%) Task-1 zero-shot success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, outperforming prompting, weight-merging, and multi-task baselines.

title: AudioTrace: File-Level Membership Detection for Audio Large Language Models
summary:
Significant privacy and copyright concerns are raised by the use of publicly available audio recordings to train audio large language models (LLMs), yet effective auditing methods remain limited.
